source_title: Kempsey's water supply now entirely reliant on rainfall
evidence_description: Reports that, amid severe drought, Willawarrin was already receiving trucked water (approx. 17,000 litres) because iron and manganese levels in the stressed Macleay River had exceeded the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines, and that Bellbrook was expected to need trucked water within a week. Describes the Macleay River as near standstill (preventing bore recharge), Steuart McIntyre Dam at approximately 80% and falling, an estimated 1,900 ML of remaining supply (about 15 months without rain), and Level 2 water restrictions in place, with Level 3 anticipated if the dam fell below 70%.
relevant_quotation: This is our last remaining water supply.
investigation_relevance: Earliest evidence located of the drought-driven water crisis that led to the 2019-2020 trucked-water period for both Willawarrin and Bellbrook; establishes the drought/river-extraction context behind the iron and manganese contamination.

source_title: Willawarrin and Bellbrook return to river supply after months of trucked-in water (media release)
evidence_description: Official council media release confirming Willawarrin and Bellbrook were switched back to river water supply on Thursday 18 June 2020, ending several months of trucked-in water. States the cause as naturally occurring iron and manganese reaching unsafe levels in the Macleay River due to the combined effects of drought, bushfire, and subsequent heavy rainfall causing soil erosion, creating potential health risk plus taste and laundry-staining complaints. States the fix was a combination of bore water and treatment processes.
relevant_quotation: There's a real sense of achievement to have Willawarrin and Bellbrook back on river
investigation_relevance: Primary/official record of the resolution of the 2019-2020 trucked-water episode; anchors the end date of that episode and the stated cause and interim fix, directly relevant to Historical failures, Trucked water, Iron contamination, and Manganese contamination.

source_title: $52.9m locked-in for landmark water infrastructure project
evidence_description: Official NSW Government announcement of a $52.9 million regional water infrastructure package: $12.5m from the Australian Government's National Water Grid Fund, $13.2m from the NSW Government's Safe and Secure Water Program, and $27.1m from Kempsey Shire Council. Primarily funds a new filtration plant treating raw water from the Steuart McIntyre Dam (2,500 ML capacity, built after the 1994 drought) and the Sherwood Borefield, serving over 18,000 residents across Kempsey, Frederickton, Smithtown, and Gladstone, with construction starting mid-2025 over an 18-month program. States this package 'builds on' the separate, already-announced $8 million Willawarrin plant ($2m NSW Government + $6m Council), serving the village's 130 residents. Quotes federal Minister Tanya Plibersek, NSW Minister Rose Jackson, and Kempsey Shire Council Mayor Kinne Ring.

investigation_relevance: Identifies the Willawarrin plant's funding as one component of a larger $52.9m regional water security program, and reveals a much larger parallel project (Steuart McIntyre Dam/Sherwood Borefield) for the main Kempsey network; also documents Mayor Kinne Ring in office by this date.

source_title: Sod turns on new $8 million Willawarrin water treatment plant

source_title: Bellbrook
evidence_description: Genuinely new historical detail for this register, from the now-preserved page: Bellbrook sits on the traditional lands of the Dunghutti people (a spelling variant of "Thunggutti", the spelling used throughout this register's Council-sourced material - not treated as a different group). It was first settled by Europeans in the mid-1830s, with "very active antagonism" between the Europeans and the Dunghutti slowing the village's development. The name "Bellbrook" was adopted in 1882 with the opening of a postal receiving office (16 January 1882; became a full post office 1 January 1884; closed 10 April 1987). Bellbrook Public School opened as a provisional school in 1883, went half-time with Pee Dee 1887-1890, closed entirely 1890-1910, was half-time with Nulla Nulla 1910-1911, and has operated continuously since 1911.
relevant_quotation: there was "very active antagonism" between the Europeans and the Dunghutti, which slowed the development of the village
investigation_relevance: Substantially deepens THR-01's pre-1900 background for Bellbrook, comparable to SRC-0036's Willawarrin settlement history. Also surfaces an unresolved, minor discrepancy worth flagging: this source dates the name "Bellbrook" to 1882 (post office naming), while EV-0018 (RUN-0033, also ultimately Wikipedia-derived) stated Bellbrook "was gazetted in 1892" - these could both be true (informal naming 1882, formal gazettal 1892) or reflect a citation drift somewhere between sources; not resolved here.
